tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. - "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Entire adversarial review

Deliver an evidence-backed review, a session visible on the intended trail, and a concrete request to publish the findings. Prefer the **Entire CLI** for trail reads, session attachment, findings, and verification. Use Git and `gh` for source and PR metadata as needed. The Entire MCP tools (`get_entire_trail`, `trail_findings`, `trail_gates`) are fine for reads; do not use them to post findings or attach sessions.

## Scope and authorization

- Explicit invocation (`/entire-adversarial-review`, or the user naming this workflow) authorizes attaching the current review session and, if necessary, pushing one empty checkpoint-link commit to the selected open trail branch. Explain each action as you take it; do not ask again when already authorized.
- Automatic skill discovery alone does not authorize transcript uploads or branch pushes. For a plain review request, complete the review first and confirm with the user before those mutations.
- Honor narrower instructions such as review-only or no pushes. Do not fix code, merge, approve, deploy, or alter unrelated branches.
- **Ask before posting findings**, unless the user already explicitly authorized posting them. Prepare the exact findings before asking. If there are none, say so without creating an empty review discussion.
- Read applicable repository instructions (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`). Respect actual validation restrictions; do not generalize one repository's prohibition on cloud or Terraform commands to other repositories.

## Review the live change

1. Resolve the project trail, repository change, branch, base, and current head SHA. Project and repository numbers differ: in `/gh/OWNER/-/trails/PROJECT_NUMBER/changes/REPO/CHANGE_NUMBER`, CLI project selection uses `PROJECT_NUMBER`, while repository API routes use `CHANGE_NUMBER`.
2. Inspect local status and preserve the user's checkout. When source or line anchoring requires it, use an isolated detached worktree at the reviewed SHA (`git worktree add --detach "$scratch/review-$sha" "$review_sha"` under the scratchpad). Refresh the remote branch before trusting local refs.
3. Read the complete diff and the smallest adjacent contracts that could invalidate it. Challenge the intended outcome: missing cases, defaults, inheritance, concurrency, retries, failure recovery, rollout ordering, and rollback behavior as relevant. Treat existing automated findings as leads, not evidence. For large diffs, fan out read-only `Explore` subagents per area, but verify every candidate finding yourself before keeping it.
4. Run focused, meaningful validation. Verify external API/provider behavior against current primary documentation. Distinguish reproduced failures from static reasoning and untested deployment behavior. Absence of findings in sampled production data does not prove an exhaustive list of enabled behavior.
5. Recheck the head before finalizing. If substantive code changed, review the delta before carrying findings forward. Separate code findings from CI, draft/conflicts, approvals, and Entire Gates.
6. Prepare each actionable finding with priority, confidence, exact file/line, trigger, impact, recommended correction, reviewed SHA, and validation boundaries. Avoid speculative findings and style-only noise.

## Attach the review session

Discover the installed CLI flags with `entire session attach --help` and `entire checkpoint explain --help`. Read the current session ID from `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (it matches the transcript `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<id>.jsonl`); never copy a session ID from an example or an earlier session.

From the target repository, preview attachment to the **reviewed commit**, not the checkout's current HEAD:

```sh
entire session attach "$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID" --agent claude-code \
  --commit "$review_sha" --review --skills entire-adversarial-review
```

Without a TTY, `attach` prints its plan and exits non-zero without changing anything — that output is the preview. Declare only skills actually used. Inspect it: which checkpoint, which commit, whether history would change, and what would be pushed. Under the authorization above, rerun with `--force` when it matches the requested operation. A pushed commit should be left unchanged. Stop if the preview would rewrite unrelated history or upload unrelated pending checkpoints; isolate the operation first.

If the sandbox blocks macOS Keychain access, rerun the same authorized command with the sandbox disabled (the user approves the prompt). Do not log in again or extract credentials. If auth errors look wrong, check `which -a git-remote-entire entire` for a stale binary first.

Verify the uploaded checkpoint by ID through the remote API:

```sh
entire checkpoint explain "$checkpoint_id" --repo "$repo_path" --json
```

Confirm the exact session ID and `kind: agent_review`. **A successful upload is not proof the trail displays the session.** The commit-SHA form of `checkpoint explain` can fail for a metadata-only link even when the checkpoint-ID form succeeds.

## Verify trail visibility; recover only if needed

Use `entire api --help` and the current API schema/source to confirm routes and field names. Resolve the repository ID for the current region; never reuse one from another session or region. The currently supported trail session query is:

```text
GET /api/v1/repos/REPO_ID/sessions?base=BASE_REF&head=TRAIL_BRANCH&limit=100
```

Call through `entire api --to cell`, URL-encode query values, and paginate when needed. Verify that the exact session ID appears in this **base/head-filtered** response. A direct session lookup or unfiltered repo listing is insufficient.

If indexing is pending, wait briefly (use `Monitor` with an until-loop, not `sleep`) and recheck with progress updates. If the checkpoint/session is retrievable but the trail list remains empty with `history_complete: true`, inspect the checkpoint's association. A known failure mode is that `session attach` records `linked_commits` metadata for an already-pushed commit, while the trail index recognizes only `Entire-Checkpoint` Git trailers. Treat this as a diagnosis to verify, not a permanent assumption about the product.

For that verified failure, use the authorized empty-commit fallback:

1. Confirm the trail is still open and the intended branch exists. Refresh its remote tip. If code moved since review, inspect the delta before proceeding.
2. Create a disposable detached worktree from the fresh tip in the scratchpad. Do not switch or modify the user's active worktree.
3. Create exactly one empty commit referencing the **existing uploaded checkpoint**:

   ```sh
   git commit --allow-empty -m 'chore: link review sessions to trail' \
     -m "Entire-Checkpoint: $checkpoint_id"
   ```

   Inspect hooks first. Preserve required checks. If an Entire capture hook would replace this deliberate trailer or capture unrelated work, isolate that hook behavior rather than silently changing the intended checkpoint. Verify the final trailer and that parent and child trees are identical (`git rev-parse HEAD^{tree} HEAD~1^{tree}`).
4. Push `HEAD:refs/heads/TRAIL_BRANCH` normally. Never force-push or amend the shared commit. If a concurrent push causes rejection, fetch and reassess; do not override it.
5. Query the trail's sessions endpoint again and verify the exact session ID appears. A checkpoint can contain multiple sessions, so this may expose all of them.
6. Refresh the trail head, findings, and gates. State that checks or approvals may restart. Remove the clean temporary worktree (`git worktree remove`) and confirm the original checkout remains unchanged.

Do not keep appending empty commits if this fails. After one verified fallback push and a bounded indexing check, report the unresolved link with checkpoint/session/head IDs and the API evidence. Do not call it complete until visibility is verified.

## Ask to publish, then post precisely

After review and attachment verification, present the concrete findings and ask **"Post these findings to the trail?"** with `AskUserQuestion` (options: post all / post a subset / don't post). This is the publication boundary requested by this workflow, not a request to approve the code. If posting was already authorized, proceed directly.

Use `entire trail finding add --help` and the current CLI. Select the project trail, repo, and branch explicitly. For example:

```sh
entire trail finding add "$project_trail" \
  --project "$project_path" --repo "$repo_path" --branch "$trail_branch" \
  --severity medium --confidence 0.94 \
  --file "$source_path" --line "$source_line" \
  --client-id "$stable_finding_key" --body "$finding_body" --json
```

Run line/range-anchored publication **from a checkout of the reviewed source** (the review worktree). The CLI hydrates `selectedText` from the local working tree even when `--branch` selects another remote branch. Posting from an unrelated checkout can silently produce the right line number with the wrong selected text. Verify returned path, line, selected text, status, and freshness. For an empty-link commit, source should be byte-identical to the reviewed parent.

Use safe argument handling for multiline bodies: write each body to a scratchpad file and pass `--body "$(cat "$body_file")"`; never interpolate untrusted text into shell code. Reuse an idempotency key only with identical fields. If a wrong-anchor copy was accidentally posted and location editing is unavailable, post a correctly anchored replacement, verify it, and dismiss only the erroneous copy with a reference to its replacement. Do not dismiss other reviewers' findings.

Report the exact reviewed head, review verdict, validation limits, session visibility, and publication status concisely. Link the trail. Never claim a session is visible merely because the push succeeded, or claim findings were posted while awaiting the user's answer.

A bootstrap that stalled while planning (INC-133) logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line (planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, branch subsumed by trunk, push attempting, branch finalized, …) now also goes to `BootstrapLogger` at Info, with the logger's own attributes; push failures and resume-marker cleanup failures go at Warn. Expect roughly two records per branch and three more per checkpoint on a batched bootstrap. `-v` output is unchanged (ENT-3751).

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.

- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.

- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

Linear: [ENT-3751](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-3751) · INC-133 follow-up

## Intent

Bootstrap planning lines never reached Datadog. During INC-133 every openclaw/openclaw attempt looked the same: a size preflight, then 30 minutes of nothing, then a timeout.

## Cause

`Params.log` wrote only to `Params.Logger`. That is the CLI's `-v` stderr text logger (`syncer.go:887`), and it is nil unless the run is verbose. The embedder's `BootstrapLogger` is wired into `PushLogger` (`syncer.go:1557`). It received only the upload diagnostic and the GitHub size lookup.

## Change

- `Params.log` writes each planning line to both `Logger` and `PushLogger`, and writes it once when they are the same logger. The worker's `BootstrapLogger` (tagged `target_ulid`, `source_owner`, `source_repo`) now carries "planning checkpoints", "fetching commit graph", "branch subsumed by trunk", "push attempting", "branch finalized" and the other planning lines.
- Push failures and resume-marker cleanup failures go to `PushLogger` at Warn. `-v` keeps Info.
- The GitHub size-lookup record still reaches `PushLogger` once, at its own level.
- `client.go` and `unstable/client.go` already pass `BootstrapLogger` through. Only their doc comments change.

`-v` output is unchanged. Volume on a batched bootstrap is about 2 records per branch plus 3 per checkpoint, at Info. This is deliberate: Debug is dropped by the collector before Datadog.

## Delivery

mirror-pipeline pins git-sync at `ca4404a3`. This needs a follow-up mirror-pipeline PR that bumps `entire.io/entire/git-sync` after merge. The worker needs no code change: it already sets `BootstrapLogger` and logs at Info.

## Tests

- `TestBootstrapPlanningLinesReachBootstrapLoggerWithoutVerbose` (syncer, end to end): planning lines reach `BootstrapLogger` with the embedder's attributes, without `-v`.
- `TestPlanningLinesReachPushLoggerWithoutVerboseLogging` covers planning lines plus the Warn level on push failure.

Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit, or to the commit named by --commit. Use this when hooks failed
to fire or weren't installed when the session started, or to attach a
research session.

How the session is linked follows from two facts about the commit — does it
already have a checkpoint, and is it pushed — the same for HEAD and --commit:
  - It already has a checkpoint: the session is added to it. Git history is
    not changed.
  - It is already pushed: the commit is left unchanged and the link is
    recorded in a new checkpoint, which is pushed right away (under the manual
    checkpoint push policy it waits for 'entire checkpoint push'). The link counts
    once the commit's author attaches it, and names that exact commit: after
    a rebase or amend, attach the session to the new commit.
  - It isn't pushed: the Entire-Checkpoint trailer is added to it, which
    rewrites it and any commits after it on the current branch (their content
    is unchanged). A trailer survives a later rebase. Merges after the commit,
    or a rebase or merge in progress, are refused. If a remote can't be
    reached to confirm the commit isn't pushed, attach refuses rather than
    risk rewriting a shared commit.

attach prints what it is about to do and asks before doing it. Without a
terminal (an agent or a script) it changes nothing and exits non-zero; show
the user what it printed, and once they agree, rerun with --force.

A session can be attached to more than one commit. Each checkpoint records the
turns since the session's previous checkpoint.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to

when it is untracked). Run 'entire agent list' to see the full list.
